papers.title: SynRec: Synergistic multi-domain recommendation with frequency-guided expert specialization
papers.abstract: Isolated, domain-specific recommender systems limit cross-domain knowledge sharing by fragmenting user behavior into data silos. Standard Multi-Domain Recommendation (MDR) methods address this by transferring knowledge across domains, but they typically rely on instance-level transfer via explicitly shared user IDs and overlapping representations. Under strict data isolation (i.e., non-overlapping users), these instance-level approaches are inapplicable. Instead, such scenarios demand structure-level transfer—sharing domain-agnostic behavioral motifs (e.g., temporal-frequency patterns) via common model parameters without requiring user identity linkage. In this work, we model non-overlapping multi-domain recommendation as a heterogeneous multi-task joint learning problem and introduce SynRec, a Transformer-based framework that uses collaborative specialization to achieve this structure-level transfer. Specifically, by redesigning the feed-forward network (FFN) as a domain-aware Mixture-of-Experts, SynRec features a hierarchical expert architecture with explicit role differentiation to decouple shared dynamics from domain-specific nuances. Furthermore, it incorporates a frequency-guided routing mechanism that utilizes the temporal-frequency decomposition of interaction sequences as domain-agnostic structural anchors to select experts adaptively, guided by a specialization-aware objective that stabilizes this division of labor and curbs negative transfer. Evaluated across six diverse, non-overlapping domains forming two distinct benchmarks, SynRec demonstrates robust generalization. It outperforms the evaluated single-domain baselines across all six domains and achieves the strongest results among the evaluated multi-domain methods on five of the six domains, demonstrating particular advantages in sparse and highly heterogeneous settings. Qualitative and quantitative analyses show the autonomous emergence of domain-adaptive specialization and facilitate rigorous model introspection into expert coordination mechanisms. Taken together, these results position collaborative specialization as a principled and efficient path for advancing multi-domain recommendation in strictly isolated environments.
papers.summary: When several businesses each run their own recommender and share no users, knowledge cannot be transferred between them through shared user IDs. This paper proposes SynRec, which lets several domains share one Transformer recommender and ==shares only domain-agnostic behavior patterns, such as the fast and slow rhythms of behavior sequences over time==. It replaces the feed-forward layer with a domain-aware mixture of experts (MoE): some experts serve all domains and learn shared patterns, while others serve only one domain and learn its differences, which limits domains dragging each other down. Across 6 domains with no shared users, it beats the single-domain models in every domain and is the best of the evaluated multi-domain methods in 5 of them.
